How Does a 401(k) Contribution Affect Your Paycheck? The $132-a-Check Answer, Worked Out Line by Line

Direct AnswerA 6% 401(k) contribution on a $65,000 salary costs $132 per biweekly check — not $150. The full rate ladder, Roth vs traditional, match math, and 2026 limits.

Gross pay estimates
By Saahil•Published November 6, 2026•12 min read•Calculation Guides
A closer look

In this guide

The Short Answer: $150 In, $132 OutWhat a 401(k) Contribution Actually IsThe Rate Ladder: What 3% to 15% Costs Per CheckThe 88-Cent Rule: What $1 Costs at Every BracketRoth vs Traditional: $150 vs $132 a CheckThe Employer Match: Free Money That Never Touches Your CheckMaxing Out: $24,500 a Year and the Catch-Up RulesStarting in July: The Mid-Year Catch-UpThe 1% Test: Raising Your Rate Without Feeling ItIf You Are Paid Hourly: $25 an Hour, Worked OutThe State Exception: Pennsylvania and MassachusettsWhere It Shows Up: Your Pay Stub and Your W-2How to Use the CalculatorLimitationsFrequently Asked QuestionsKey Takeaways & Action Plan

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Quick Answer

A 6% 401(k) contribution on a $65,000 salary costs $132.00 per biweekly check — not $150.00. The $150.00 goes into your retirement account, but your federal income tax falls by $18.00 a check, so your take-home pay drops by only $132.00. Social Security and Medicare do not move at all: FICA is charged on your full $2,500.00 gross either way. The rule behind it is simple — at a 12% marginal tax rate, every $1 you contribute to a traditional 401(k) costs $0.88 of take-home pay. A Roth contribution costs the full $1.00, because it never reduces your taxable income.

The Short Answer: $150 In, $132 Out

The question behind this guide is the one people actually type: "how much does a 401(k) reduce my paycheck?" The answer is almost never the contribution itself. A traditional 401(k) contribution is taken out of your pay before federal income tax is calculated, so the tax you would have paid on that money never leaves your check — and your paycheck shrinks by the contribution minus the tax saved. The formula is one line: take-home drop = contribution − income tax saved.

Here is the whole answer on one worker — $65,000 a year, paid biweekly, single filer in 2026, no state tax — worked out step by step at 6%:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay per check$65,000.00 ÷ 26$2,500.00
Step 2 — 401(k) contribution per check6% × $2,500.00$150.00
Step 3 — Federal tax before the 401(k)$5,620.00 ÷ 26$216.15
Step 4 — Federal tax after the 401(k)$5,152.00 ÷ 26$198.15
Step 5 — Income tax saved per check$216.15 − $198.15$18.00
Step 6 — Take-home drop per check$150.00 − $18.00$132.00

Take-home pay goes from $2,092.60 a check to $1,960.60 a check. Over the year that is $3,900.00 into the plan for a $3,432.00 take-home cost, with $468.00 of federal tax you simply never pay. The honesty note: this is a federal-only sketch for a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction. State income tax, in most states, saves a little more — Pennsylvania and Massachusetts are the exceptions, and they get their own section below. Our 401(k) paycheck impact calculator runs the same trade-off at your salary and your rate, and our paycheck calculator shows the full check with every line.

What a 401(k) Contribution Actually Is

A 401(k) contribution is an elective deferral: you tell your employer to send part of each paycheck straight into a retirement account instead of into your bank account, and the money never passes through your hands. You choose either a percentage of pay — the usual way, 3% or 6% or 10% — or a flat dollar amount per check, and payroll applies it every pay period until you change it.

The part people get wrong is which taxes it escapes. A traditional pre-tax contribution is excluded from the wages used to calculate federal income tax (and, in most states, state income tax), but it is not excluded from the wages used for Social Security and Medicare. That split is why the paycheck drop is smaller than the contribution but never zero: you save the income-tax slice and keep paying the FICA slice. A Roth 401(k) contribution is the mirror image — it comes out after income tax, so it saves no tax today at all, and the payoff is tax-free withdrawals in retirement. The table below is the whole mechanism in one place:

Paycheck lineTraditional 401(k)Roth 401(k)No contribution
Gross pay per check$2,500.00$2,500.00$2,500.00
Income-tax wages (Box 1 basis)$2,350.00$2,500.00$2,500.00
FICA wages (Boxes 3 and 5 basis)$2,500.00$2,500.00$2,500.00
Federal income tax withheld$198.15$216.15$216.15
FICA withheld (7.65%)$191.25$191.25$191.25
401(k) contribution$150.00$150.00$0.00
Take-home pay$1,960.60$1,942.60$2,092.60

Two things to notice. First, the FICA line is $191.25 in all three columns — that is the most common error in quick 401(k) calculators, which subtract the deferral from FICA wages and understate the paycheck hit by 7.65% of the contribution. Second, the traditional and Roth columns differ by exactly $18.00 a check, the income tax the traditional contribution saves. That $18.00 is not free money: the $150.00 you deferred will be taxed as ordinary income when you withdraw it in retirement. What you are buying with it is decades of tax-deferred growth plus the employer match, which is the next section but one. Our FICA guide explains the 7.65% layer in full, and our pay-stub guide shows where the 401(k) line sits on a real stub.

The Rate Ladder: What 3% to 15% Costs Per Check

The same $65,000 worker, the same biweekly schedule, at four contribution rates. Every row is computed the same way — taxable income is gross minus the contribution minus the $16,100 standard deduction, federal tax follows the 2026 brackets (10% to $12,400 of taxable income, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700), and FICA is 7.65% of the full $65,000 in every row:

RateIn per checkFederal tax / checkTake-home / checkDrop / checkTax saved / check
0%$0.00$216.15$2,092.60$0.00$0.00
3%$75.00$207.15$2,026.60$66.00$9.00
6%$150.00$198.15$1,960.60$132.00$18.00
10%$250.00$186.15$1,872.60$220.00$30.00
15%$375.00$171.15$1,762.60$330.00$45.00

The ladder has a clean pattern, and it is the pattern that makes the whole guide easy to remember: at this income, every rate costs exactly 88% of the contribution in take-home pay. Three percent costs $66.00 of the $75.00, six percent costs $132.00 of the $150.00, fifteen percent costs $330.00 of the $375.00. That is because the worker's marginal federal rate is 12% at every one of these rates — the contribution never pushes taxable income across a bracket line — so the tax saving is always 12 cents on the dollar and the cost is always 88 cents. The annual version of the same table: 3% puts $1,950.00 in for a $1,716.00 take-home cost, 6% puts $3,900.00 in for $3,432.00, 10% puts $6,500.00 in for $5,720.00, and 15% puts $9,750.00 in for $8,580.00. If your marginal rate is different, the pattern holds with a different percentage — which is the next section.

The 88-Cent Rule: What $1 Costs at Every Bracket

Your cost per dollar contributed is one minus your marginal income-tax rate — and only your income-tax rate, never FICA, because FICA never changes. Federal only, before any state saving:

Your marginal federal bracketTax saved per $1Take-home cost per $1What $150 a check costs
10%$0.10$0.90$135.00
12% (the $65,000 anchor)$0.12$0.88$132.00
22%$0.22$0.78$117.00
24%$0.24$0.76$114.00

The 22% row is worth working out, because it is where the rule starts to feel generous. Take a single filer at $78,000 a year, $3,000.00 per biweekly check, contributing 6% — $180.00 a check, $4,680.00 a year. Without the contribution, taxable income is $61,900.00 and federal tax is $8,330.00. With it, taxable income is $57,220.00 and federal tax is $7,300.40. The saving is $1,029.60 a year, $39.60 a check, so the $180.00 contribution costs only $140.40 a check in take-home pay — $3,650.40 for the year instead of $4,680.00. The same $150.00-a-check contribution that costs $132.00 in the 12% bracket costs $117.00 in the 22% bracket. One warning about the table: it uses your marginal rate, the rate on your last dollar, not your effective rate. A calculator that multiplies the contribution by your effective rate — say 17% when your marginal rate is 22% — understates the saving and overstates the paycheck hit, which is exactly the error one of the top-ranking 401(k) calculators makes (see the competitor note in the methodology box). If you live in a state with income tax, add your state marginal rate to the saving: at 22% federal plus 5% state, a dollar costs about $0.73.

Roth vs Traditional: $150 vs $132 a Check

The same 6% on the same $65,000 salary, two different accounts. The traditional contribution costs $132.00 a check in take-home pay. The Roth contribution costs the full $150.00 — $18.00 more per check, $468.00 more per year — because Roth money is taxed going in and the withholding never drops. Annual take-home: $50,975.50 traditional, $50,507.50 Roth.

That $468.00 a year is the price of the Roth's payoff: qualified withdrawals in retirement, including every dollar of growth, come out tax-free, while every dollar withdrawn from a traditional 401(k) is taxed as ordinary income. Which one wins depends on a rate you cannot know today — your tax rate in retirement versus your rate now. Two rules of thumb cover most cases. If your rate now is low — you are early in your career, or in the 10% or 12% bracket — the Roth is cheap insurance, because you are paying 12 cents to protect growth that might otherwise be taxed at 22 cents or more. If your rate now is high and you expect it to fall in retirement, the traditional contribution's bigger paycheck saving usually wins. And one practical point: the $24,500 annual limit counts your pre-tax and Roth deferrals together, so splitting between the two does not raise the ceiling — it only changes how much of the $24,500 is taxed now versus later. Our bonus-tax guide shows the same traditional-versus-Roth choice on a one-off $10,000 bonus, where the deferral decision has to be made before the money is paid.

The Employer Match: Free Money That Never Touches Your Check

The employer match is the only part of a 401(k) that adds money without subtracting any. It never passes through your paycheck: your employer sends it straight into the plan on top of your contribution, so it cannot change any take-home number in this guide. The most common formula is 50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of your pay. On a $65,000 salary at a 6% contribution, that is $1,950.00 a year — $75.00 per biweekly check — of employer money on top of your $3,900.00. Total into the plan: $5,850.00 a year, for a $3,432.00 take-home cost. You put in $3,900.00, your paycheck falls $3,432.00, and the account grows by $5,850.00.

The match is also the most expensive thing to leave behind. Contribute only 3% under the same formula and the match is $975.00 — half the $1,950.00 — so you leave $975.00 a year on the table to save $1,716.00 of take-home pay. The trade, in one line: raising the contribution from 3% to 6% costs $66.00 more per check and buys $150.00 more of your own money plus $75.00 more of match — $225.00 a check into the plan for $66.00 out of the check. Another common formula is tiered: 100% on the first 3% of pay, then 50% on the next 2%. At a 5% contribution on $65,000 that pays $1,950.00 plus $650.00 — $2,600.00 a year, $100.00 a check — on top of your $3,250.00. Whichever formula your plan uses, the rule is the same: contribute at least up to the cap, because below the cap every extra dollar you defer is matched, and above the cap it is not. The match does not count toward your $24,500 employee limit, and it is usually subject to a vesting schedule — leave before you are vested and some of the match can come back out, which is worth checking before you count it as yours.

Maxing Out: $24,500 a Year and the Catch-Up Rules

For 2026 the IRS caps your own elective deferrals at $24,500 a year — up from $23,500 in 2025 — and that number is the same whether your deferrals are traditional, Roth, or split between the two. On a $65,000 salary, maxing out means deferring 37.7% of pay, $942.31 per biweekly check. The paycheck math at the limit, single filer, federal only:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Annual deferral$24,500.00 ÷ 26 checks$942.31 per check
Step 2 — Taxable income$65,000.00 − $24,500.00 − $16,100.00$24,400.00
Step 3 — Federal income tax$1,240.00 + 12% × $12,000.00$2,680.00 a year
Step 4 — FICA (unchanged)$65,000.00 × 7.65%$4,972.50 a year
Step 5 — Take-home pay$65,000.00 − $24,500.00 − $2,680.00 − $4,972.50$32,847.50 a year ($1,263.37 a check)
Step 6 — Take-home cost of maxing out$54,407.50 − $32,847.50$21,560.00 a year ($829.23 a check)

Maxing out costs $21,560.00 of take-home pay to put $24,500.00 into the plan — the $2,940.00 difference is federal tax you never pay, and the cost per dollar is still $0.88, because the whole deferral sits inside the 12% bracket. For most people at this income, $942.31 a check is not realistic, and it does not need to be: the limit is a ceiling, not a target. The catch-up rules raise the ceiling for older workers:

Your age in 2026Regular limitCatch-upYour totalPer biweekly check
Under 50$24,500—$24,500$942.31
50 to 59, and 64 or older$24,500$8,000$32,500$1,250.00
60 to 63$24,500$11,250$35,750$1,375.00

At $65,000, a 50-year-old maxing out with the catch-up defers $32,500.00 — exactly half the salary — and take-home falls to $25,807.50 a year, $992.60 a check, a $1,100.00-a-check cost. Two 2026 details matter here. First, the higher $11,250 catch-up for ages 60 to 63 comes from the SECURE 2.0 Act, and at 64 it drops back to $8,000. Second, starting in 2026, if your FICA wages from the employer sponsoring the plan were over $150,000 in the prior year, your catch-up contributions must be made as Roth — pre-tax catch-ups are no longer available to those higher earners. The employer match does not count toward any of these limits; the combined employee-plus-employer limit is $72,000 a year, and the match can only be figured on up to $360,000 of salary.

Starting in July: The Mid-Year Catch-Up

Most people do not start contributing on January 1. They start at open enrollment, after a raise, or halfway through the year — and the mid-year math is the question competitors never answer. Say you start in July, with 13 biweekly checks left in the year, and you want the full 6% year of $3,900.00. Spreading it over 13 checks means $300.00 a check, and at the 12% marginal rate the take-home cost is $264.00 a check for the rest of the year — double the $132.00 it would have cost spread over 26 checks, but the same $3,432.00 total for the year.

The alternative is to keep the contribution at 6% of each remaining check — $150.00 a check, $1,950.00 for the year — and accept that the other $1,950.00 of deferral room is gone. You cannot retroactively defer pay you already received: a contribution only applies to paychecks not yet paid. What you can do is raise the percentage on the remaining checks to fill the room, as long as the plan allows it and the total stays under the $24,500 limit. The same logic applies to a bonus: deferring from a bonus has to be elected before the bonus is paid, which is why our bonus-tax guide prices the election before payday. And if you change jobs mid-year, the $24,500 limit follows you, not the plan — deferrals at both employers count toward the same ceiling, so add them up before you set the new percentage.

The 1% Test: Raising Your Rate Without Feeling It

If 6% feels like a jump, do not jump — step. Raising your contribution by one percentage point on a $65,000 salary adds $650.00 a year to the plan, $25.00 per biweekly check, and costs only $22.00 a check in take-home pay, because the 12% tax saving covers $3.00 of every $25.00. Over a year that is $650.00 saved for $572.00 of spending given up, with $78.00 of federal tax you never pay — and if your employer matches at 50% up to 6%, half of that extra 1% is matched too, so the plan actually gains $37.50 a check for a $22.00 cost.

The 1% test is also the honest way to find your real limit. Raise the rate by 1%, live with it for two or three pay periods, and see whether anything in your budget actually breaks. Most people find the $22.00 disappears into spending they never notice — a takeout order, a streaming add-on — and then they raise it another point. Three raises of 1% take you from 3% to 6% over a few months, at $22.00 a check each, instead of one $66.00-a-check jump on a single payday. The reverse works the same way: if money gets tight, dropping the rate by 1% puts $22.00 a check back in your pocket immediately, and the change takes effect in one or two pay periods. The one move to avoid is dropping below the match cap to solve a short-term squeeze — that trades $22.00 a check of spending for $37.50 a check of retirement money, and the match you give up never comes back.

If You Are Paid Hourly: $25 an Hour, Worked Out

Hourly workers get the same deal, priced per week instead of per check. At $25.00 an hour, 40 hours a week, 52 weeks a year, gross pay is $52,000.00. A 6% contribution is $60.00 a week, $3,120.00 a year. Without it, federal tax is $4,060.00 and FICA is $3,978.00, for take-home of $43,962.00 a year — the same figure our $25-an-hour guide computes. With it, taxable income falls to $32,780.00, federal tax to $3,685.60, and take-home to $41,216.40. The cost is $52.80 a week, $2,745.60 a year — again $0.88 per dollar, because the 12% marginal rate does the same work at any pay level.

Two things are different for hourly pay. First, the contribution is a percentage of each check, so it scales automatically: an overtime week means a bigger contribution and a bigger tax saving in the same week, and a short week means a smaller one — you never have to adjust the percentage when the hours move. Second, the match is usually figured on pay, not hours, so overtime pay can earn match money too, up to the plan's cap. If your hours vary a lot, the percentage method is the right choice; a flat dollar amount per check over-contributes on short weeks and under-contributes on long ones. Run your own rate and hours through our 401(k) impact calculator, and compare the result with our $25-an-hour guide to see the same take-home figure from the other side.

The State Exception: Pennsylvania and Massachusetts

In most states with an income tax, a traditional 401(k) contribution lowers your state taxable income just as it lowers your federal one — which means the take-home cost in those states is smaller than the federal-only figures in this guide. Two states break the pattern. Pennsylvania taxes 401(k) contributions at the state level in the year you make them: the state treats them as taxable compensation, so on the $65,000 anchor at 6%, you still pay Pennsylvania's flat 3.07% on the $3,900.00 — $119.73 a year that a worker in a conforming state never pays. Massachusetts does the same at its 5% rate, $195.00 a year on the same contribution.

Pennsylvania's sting has a silver lining: because the state already taxed the money going in, it does not tax 401(k) withdrawals in retirement — at the state level, a Pennsylvania 401(k) behaves like a Roth. Massachusetts has no such offset on withdrawals. The practical consequence is small but real: in Pennsylvania, the traditional-versus-Roth choice is decided on federal tax alone, because the state treats both the same. In the nine states with no personal income tax at all — Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming — the state question is moot, and the federal-only figures in this guide are the whole story.

Where It Shows Up: Your Pay Stub and Your W-2

You can check this whole guide against two documents you already have. On a pay stub, the 401(k) line sits with the deductions, and the tell is the three wage bases: gross pay, the FICA wage base, and the income-tax wage base. Our pay-stub guide works a full stub where a 5% 401(k) contribution of $120.40 lowers the income-tax wages but leaves the FICA wages untouched — the same asymmetry this guide prices. If your stub shows FICA calculated on pay after the 401(k), the stub is wrong, and that is worth $11.48 a check on the $150.00 contribution above (7.65% of $150.00).

On the W-2, the contribution shows up in three places. Box 1, wages for federal income tax, is gross minus the deferral: $65,000.00 minus $3,900.00 is $61,100.00. Box 3, Social Security wages, and Box 5, Medicare wages, stay at the full $65,000.00 — the FICA bases again. And Box 12, code D, reports the $3,900.00 itself, so you can confirm the year's total without adding up 26 stubs. One more thing the W-2 shows: your refund. The $18.00 a check of federal tax you did not have withheld is $468.00 over the year, which means your tax refund will be $468.00 smaller (or the amount you owe $468.00 larger) than it would have been without the contribution. The saving is real — it arrived in your paychecks all year instead of in a single refund check, which is the better place for it to be.

How to Use the Calculator

Price your own 401(k) in four steps:

  1. Step 1 — Enter your salary and your contribution percentage in the 401(k) impact calculator, with your pay frequency — biweekly is the most common, and the calculator works per check.
  2. Step 2 — Read the take-home reduction, not the contribution: that is the number your budget feels, and it is smaller than the contribution by your marginal tax rate.
  3. Step 3 — Add your employer match — the match rate and the cap percentage — and check whether your contribution reaches the cap. Below the cap, every extra point earns free money.
  4. Step 4 — Test the next step before you take it: raise the rate by 1% in the calculator and read the new take-home cost. If it is $22.00 a check or less at your income, it is a step you can take this month.

Limitations

  1. Federal only unless stated: every take-home figure uses 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction. State and local taxes are excluded except where the state section names them, so actual take-home is lower in most states — and the Pennsylvania and Massachusetts figures are the exception, not the rule.
  2. One filer, one situation: married filing jointly, head of household, other income, tax credits, and multiple jobs all change the brackets and the saving. The $0.88-per-dollar rule holds only while your marginal rate stays at 12%.
  3. Withholding is not your final tax: the $18.00-a-check saving is tax not withheld, not tax finally owed. Your return settles the difference, so your refund will be $468.00 smaller at the 6% anchor — the saving is real, it just arrives per check instead of at filing.
  4. Plan rules vary: vesting schedules, match formulas, whether bonuses and overtime count toward the match, loan and hardship-withdrawal rules, and Roth availability all differ by plan. The match figures here use the most common formulas; your plan document governs.
  5. High earners face different lines: Social Security tax stops at the $184,500 wage base, the additional 0.9% Medicare tax starts at $200,000 in wages, and from 2026 catch-up contributions must be Roth for workers whose prior-year FICA wages exceeded $150,000. The figures here do not cross those lines.
  6. Not tax or financial advice: these are 2026 federal estimates for a single filer taking the standard deduction, using the same method as the site's other guides. Investment returns, fees, and your retirement tax rate are not modeled, and the right contribution for you depends on your whole budget.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about 401(k) contributions and their paycheck:

How much does a 401(k) reduce my paycheck?

Less than the contribution, if it is a traditional pre-tax 401(k). On a $65,000 salary paid biweekly, a 6% contribution puts $150.00 into the plan each check but take-home falls by only $132.00, because the contribution saves $18.00 of federal income tax per check. At a 12% marginal rate, every $1 you contribute costs $0.88 of take-home pay; at 22% it costs $0.78. A Roth 401(k) contribution costs the full amount, because it does not reduce your taxable income.

Does a 401(k) reduce Social Security and Medicare taxes?

No. A traditional 401(k) contribution is excluded from federal (and usually state) income-tax wages, but it is still included in Social Security and Medicare wages under Internal Revenue Code §3121. On a $65,000 salary the FICA charge stays $4,972.50 a year — $191.25 per biweekly check — whether you contribute 0% or 15%. The one common deduction that does cut FICA is a Section 125 health insurance premium, which is why the two lines behave differently on a pay stub.

Is a Roth 401(k) better than a traditional 401(k) for my paycheck?

For your paycheck today, traditional wins: the same 6% on a $65,000 salary costs $132.00 a check traditional and $150.00 a check Roth — $468.00 more a year out of your pocket for the Roth. The Roth pays you back later, because qualified withdrawals in retirement, including all the growth, are tax-free, while traditional withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income. If you expect your tax rate in retirement to be higher than it is now, the Roth can still be the better deal despite the bigger paycheck hit.

How much should I contribute to get the full employer match?

At least up to the cap in your plan's match formula. The most common formula is 50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of your pay: on a $65,000 salary that is a $1,950.00-a-year match for a $3,900.00 contribution. Contribute only 3% and the match is $975.00 — you leave $975.00 a year on the table. The match never passes through your paycheck at all: it goes straight into the plan, so it costs you nothing in take-home pay and it does not count toward your $24,500 employee limit.

What is the 2026 401(k) contribution limit?

For 2026 the IRS employee elective-deferral limit is $24,500, up from $23,500 in 2025. Workers age 50 and older can add an $8,000 catch-up, for $32,500 in total, and workers who turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 during 2026 can add $11,250 instead, for $35,750. On a $65,000 salary, maxing out means deferring 37.7% of pay — $942.31 per biweekly check. The limit covers your own pre-tax and Roth deferrals combined; the employer match does not count toward it, and the combined employee-plus-employer limit is $72,000.

Can I change my 401(k) contribution during the year?

Yes, in most plans you can change your contribution percentage at any time, and the change usually takes effect in one or two pay periods. That is how a mid-year start works: if you begin in July with 13 biweekly checks left, deferring $300.00 a check still reaches a full 6% year ($3,900.00), at a $264.00-a-check take-home cost for the rest of the year. Two limits: you cannot reclassify money you already received, and a bonus deferral must be elected before the bonus is paid — after payday it is too late.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • A 6% 401(k) contribution on a $65,000 salary costs $132.00 per biweekly check, not $150.00 — the $18.00 difference is federal income tax you never pay, and FICA stays $191.25 a check either way.
  • Every $1 costs $1 minus your marginal income-tax rate — $0.88 at 12%, $0.78 at 22%, $0.90 at 10% — and never less than that, because FICA is charged on your full pay.
  • Roth costs the full $150.00 a check where traditional costs $132.00 — $468.00 more a year out of pocket — and the payoff is tax-free withdrawals in retirement, not a smaller bill today.
  • Contribute at least to the match cap — at 50% up to 6%, a 6% contribution buys $1,950.00 a year of employer money, and contributing only 3% leaves $975.00 a year on the table.
  • Maxing out in 2026 means $24,500 a year, $942.31 a biweekly check — a $21,560.00 take-home cost on a $65,000 salary — with $32,500 at age 50+ and $35,750 at ages 60 to 63.
  • Starting in July still works — $300.00 a check for the 13 checks left reaches the full $3,900.00 year at a $264.00-a-check cost, but you cannot defer pay you already received.
  • The 1% test is the way to raise your rate — $25.00 more into the plan costs $22.00 a check in take-home pay, and two or three pay periods will tell you whether your budget even notices.
  • Check your W-2 — Box 1 should be gross minus the deferral ($61,100.00 on the anchor), Boxes 3 and 5 the full gross, and Box 12 code D the $3,900.00 total; if FICA was calculated after the 401(k), the stub is wrong.

Sources & Method

Contribution limits: IRS news release IR-2025-111 and Notice 2025-67 — 2026 employee elective-deferral limit $24,500, catch-up $8,000 (age 50+), enhanced catch-up $11,250 (ages 60–63), combined employee-plus-employer limit $72,000, compensation cap $360,000; SECURE 2.0 Roth catch-up rule for prior-year FICA wages over $150,000, effective 2026. Tax figures: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 — 2026 standard deduction $16,100 (single), brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700, 24% to $201,775 of taxable income; FICA 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%), per IRS Topic No. 424 and IRC §3121. Withholding follows the IRS Publication 15-T percentage method. State treatment: Pennsylvania taxes 401(k) contributions at its flat 3.07% (Pennsylvania Department of Revenue) and exempts withdrawals; Massachusetts taxes contributions at 5%. Cross-checks: the rate ladder matches paycheckscalculator.org's independently computed ladder to the cent ($2,092.60 / $2,026.60 / $1,960.60 / $1,872.60 / $1,762.60 per check); the $60,000, 10% example matches the site's own 401(k) impact calculator ($1,938.08 without, $1,735.00 with); the $65,000 no-contribution take-home of $54,407.50 matches the site's corrected hourly-vs-salary guide; the $25-an-hour take-home of $43,962.00 matches the site's $25-an-hour guide. Competitor note: paycheckscalculator.org (top result, updated Oct 31, 2026) has the same per-check ladder but no Roth comparison, no match pricing, no max-out or catch-up math, no mid-year start, and no state exceptions; timeclock44.com uses an effective-rate shortcut that gives $124.50 instead of the correct $132.00 per check and a take-home baseline that does not match Pub 15-T math; paycalc.online still shows the stale 2025 limit of $23,500 and wrongly reduces FICA in its example table; legalclarity.org explains the mechanism well but gives no worked per-check ladder. This article is general information, not tax or financial advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. A traditional 401(k) contribution costs less than the contribution itself — $132.00 a check for $150.00 in at 6% on a $65,000 salary — because the income tax on that money never leaves your check, while FICA is charged on your full pay either way.
  2. Contribute at least up to your employer's match cap: at 50% up to 6%, a 6% contribution buys $1,950.00 a year of employer money, and stopping at 3% leaves $975.00 a year on the table.
  3. The 2026 limit is $24,500 — $942.31 a biweekly check to max out — with $32,500 at age 50+ and $35,750 at ages 60 to 63; if 6% feels like a jump, raise your rate 1% at a time at $22.00 a check.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 6, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
